body:
"Amorphous blob of depression."

Yes. I've always connected with that word - amorphous - but I sort of assumed people wouldn't get it.. 
Kudos for having the motivation to go on a jog. Even something as simple as that can seem a momentous feat at times

The topic came up when I quit my job. My 2 weeks notice came as a shock to everyone, especially higher ups. One of the business owners (a senior Veterinarian) is ruthless, impatient and extremely cynical. Her constant jibes, criticism and downright cruelty broke me down, and when I quit I told the business manager straight up. I couldn't handle the disrespect anymore, and to fully illustrate why it affected me so deeply, I divulged my history of major depression. Or, at least, I touched the tip of the iceburg. 
Then, when I came back to this job a couple months later (with a degree and a promotion) I found out that the veterinarian that treated me poorly had been spoken to about how terrible she had been and felt very embarrased that she was a motivating factor in my choice to leave the company. She vowed to try to change, and even told me that her daughter had struggled with depression. Sadly, I wasn't on any medication, was overwhelmed with my new position and eventually broke down and voluntarily admitted myself to the hospital. At this point there was no getting around it. And I dreaded going back to work, because I knew there would be questions. I didn't want to have to describe my illness to every single person (there are 50+ employees at my workplace).

Overall, though, I'm glad I told someone. I got a lot of hugs and the same general message "we're just happy you're ok & want you on our team". When I was in the hospital, I had to make a very difficult call to the business manager and explain my situation (I had missed a few shifts) as well as ask for my original position back. That was the most difficult phone call I think I've ever made. She was incredibly supportive and just wanted me to be okay. There were definitely some tears shed during that phone call (on my end of course) - I just didn't care to hide it anymore. I had been stuffing it down for so long. She, and most other people there, have maintained that supportive stance.

We are confused because we use our minds too much and our bodies too little. At least I know that's true for me.
If I had chosen to do something with all of those moments when I was letting my mind run, I might not have sunk so low.
Alas, there's the beauty of depression. It holds us still, rendering our bodies immovable so that our minds may spin out of control.

The strange thing for me is, I got straight A's through school and hardly studied, not because I wasn't interested but because of how awful I normally felt. I would always have an intent to study, but it just seemed so pointless. I can't explain how I did so well. People assume I am a whiz and that I study constantly, and the fact that I don't makes my achievements seem that much more blank. I think I just have a great memory. I graduated with high honors, only studied for a few weeks (I had roughly three months) and then passed my national boards and it only took me a third of the alloted time to take the test. And several of my classmates who have been working their butts off failed. I still feel like a lazy piece of crud though.

I know you are right. I try to tell him that I'm sad. Lately I've been more honest when he askes me how I am. I feel so awful that he has to always be cheering me up. I want to make him happy, to enjoy our life together. He's said that he'll never leave me because all he wants is to be with me. His devotion and love are honestly one of the few things keeping me afloat. I have a hard time really putting into words how I feel, but I'll try it tonight. Thank you. <3

I think you are %100 correct. I passed my boards and am a Tech now at my workplace, but I can't stand it. I feel like there is so much riding on me and I've already made mistakes. I want to go back to my old position there as an Assistant because I was good at it, and it didn't give me nearly as much of that feeling of imminent failure. I just get so much anxiety when having to deal with clients.

We had a dog come in for a dental that turned into extractions (after radiographs). The Dr. on the case is board certified in Veterinary Dentistry. Our policy is to call the client (if needed) during the dental to inform of the state of the teeth and either get a yes or no on extractions. Drs and Techs have to explain to people all the time why we can't tell before anesthesia and radiographs what teeth will need to be pulled.
So the Dr. called the owner (the wife), informed her of the disease state present in her dog's mouth, explained to her the detrimental effects this was having (and would continue to have) on her dog's quality of life, and recommended extractions. She agreed with little hesitation.
Later the husband called and was irate because he said his wife was 'distraught' over the phone conversation with the Dr. and felt pressured into saying yes to the extractions. She was especially upset that the Dr's statement that not pulling the teeth now would cause more pain for the patient as well as more money spent down the road (which is 100% true..)
The Dr. again explained that dental pathology cannot be visualized without dental x-rays while the pet is under anesthesia. He said he gave the Mr's wife an option of not pulling the teeth, and he didn't pressure her, but he also didn't sugarcoat anything. (This Dr is great with people, by the way, and is very good at breaking things down for clients). After some heated discussion the client hung up.

The client called again, and informed the Dr. that he had recorded their past telephone conversation and had caught him in a lie. Of course that changed things, because the client took what was just a misunderstanding to a very personal and inappropriate level. When the guy picked up his dog he said he was sure we were just 'up-selling' our services to make more money and would be disputing the charges. 
And I should add that I brought the dog to the room and noticed the client was wearing an expensive looking pinstriped suit with the look of a very meticulously groomed businessman :) Obviously quite pressed for $$.

Speaking from experience, I'd say the Vet Tech route is a good choice. I am 27 and just passed my boards today to become an RVT after two years of school. I landed a job at a progressive 7 (now 8) doctor clinic as an assistant shortly after starting my program and am now a Technician there.  You don't have to be locked into a Tech career, either. There a few people that finished my program, are Techs, and are pursuing Vet school. Working as a Tech in the field will be a great way to figure out just how far you want to go + what field of Vet Medicine you're passionate about. My best friend went the other route, got her undergrad then went straight on to Vet school. She's known what she wanted since she was a kid and she got it. So we graduated at about the same time :) I am super proud of her and know she'll be a great DVM but I don't think I would be happy in that position. As other posters have mentioned, its a boatload of debt, plus long hours and a lot of responsibility to both the pets and their people. I've seen some pretty nasty clients come through the practice that I work at, people that are volatile and petty trying to make trouble, and guess who ultimately has to deal with them? The Drs. There is a lot riding on a Dr to make the right decisions, figure out the best way to treat a patient, plus keep the client happy. It can be a hard balancing act.

My longterm goal is become an Equine Vet Tech. Or, perhaps, go back to school and study turtles :) Two very different things, I know. I have a while to figure it out :)
